offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also liable to fine
physical_harm: The deceased committed suicide, but no specific injuries or death caused by the accused are mentioned
number_of_offences: Four offences/counts charged, but none were finally upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning to drive the deceased to commit suicide
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the deceased was pained and disturbed due to the husband's illicit affair with appellant No.4, but found no evidence of mental cruelty sufficient to satisfy the first limb of Section 498A IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, but noted discrepancies in the documents presented by the prosecution, which were not believed by the trial judge and the High Court.
bail_history: As they are on bail, they be discharged of their bail bonds
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed by the High Court of Gujarat on 09.07.2008, and the Supreme Court decision was on FEBRUARY 18, 2015
legal_representation: Harish Raichura, learned counsel for the appellants and Anurag Ahluwalia, learned counsel for the State
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed under Sections 498A, 306 and Section 201 read with Section 114 of the Indian Penal Code
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Jamnagar; High Court: Affirmed the conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased committed suicide due to cruelty inflicted by her husband and his relatives, including an extra-marital relationship, which led to marital discord and financial exploitation. The prosecution also alleged that the deceased was driven out of her home and compelled to stay on the terrace, leading to her suicide.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was a divorce between the deceased and her husband, and that she was staying on the terrace of the house, having committed suicide by consuming poison. They contended that the accused had no role in her death and that the evidence of cruelty was not sufficient to sustain the charges.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that mere extra-marital relationship, even if proved, would be illegal and immoral unless it was shown that the accused conducted in such a manner as to drive the wife to commit suicide. The Court emphasized that the first limb of Section 498A IPC refers to cruelty, not dowry demand.
precedent_relied_upon: Pinakin Mahipatray Rawal v. State of Gujarat 2013 (10) SCR 306 = 2013 (10) SCC 48; Girdhar Shankar Tawade v. State of Maharashtra 2002 (3) SCR 376 = 2002 (5) SCC 177; Gurnaib Singh v. State of Punjab 2013 (3) SCR 563 = 2013 (7) SCC 108
